Omicron House of 1910
Thirty-five years after the founding of the Univer
sity of Illinois in 1868 the first steps were taken by six
members of the CoUege of Engineering to establish
the Omicron Chapter, the twenty-fourth crowm in
the diadem of Psi Upsilon. It took eight years for this
to progress from a small club to the Chapter as it is
known today.
Six young men, led by Emmett L. Murphy '07 be
gan to explore what was missing from their lives as
undergraduates. Some felt that they had not come to
the attention of the existing clubs and fraternities on
campus or had overlooked the opportunity to have
joined one of those then existing there. They did
realize, however, that there was much to be gained by
living together, sharing the problems of a home op
erated and managed by themselves and the oppor
tunities to meet and know others better. This was cer
tainly not part of the existence in the college dormi
tories and scattered living places.
Thus, in 1903, these six had each gathered into the
group one other undergraduate until there were twelve
young men with a desire for fellowship and the in
terchange of responsibilities. After several meetings
in the members' rooms, the Aztec Club was organized
and officers duly elected. The year was 1904. The
name Aztec did not have any particular significance.
It was the second choice of the group after another
name had been suggested. It was learned the first
name suggested was used quite frequently in the
Greek Letter Societies and thus seemed one to avoid.
While the group had every name from A to Z from
which to pick, Aztec was the final selection.
When the Aztec Club made its presence knovra on
the campus in 1904 speculation was immediate that
it had been formed for the sole purpose of attracting
a chapter of some national fraternity to the Illinois
campus. While this feeling was held by members of
the established fraternities at the university it was
not the intention of the Aztec Club membership. How
ever, the idea did begin to gain acceptance within the
membership of the Aztec Club and took its original
form when a professor at the university, who was an
alumnus of Delta Kappa Epsilon, suggested that the
fraternity turn to Psi Upsilon.
During the period from 1904 to 1905 the members
of the Aztec Club had determined that, if they were
to affiliate with any national fraternity, it would be
Psi Upsilon and, if this was not possible, they would
remain as the Aztec Club. The only member of Psi
Upsilon, Dr. Charles M. Moss, Pi '77, who started out
as a rather lukewarm supporter of the idea of the af
filiation of the Aztec Club with Psi Upsilon, became
one of the ardent supporters of the project when it

By the time 1906 rolled around the members of
the Aztec Club had pursued every lead possible to
establish themselves as
worthy of consideration as a
chapter of Psi Upsilon. They realized that their first
efforts must prove to the midwestern Chapters that
they were worthy of serious consideration. This cam
paign was carried on at the highest levels of dignity
by members of the Aztec Club who were well pre
pared to plead their case and invite any form of in
spection that any Chapter or Alumni Association in
the area wanted to conduct.
These repeated invitations to come and see what
was on the campus of the University of Illinois under
the aegis of the Aztec Club generated a series of such
inspections and visits with the membership. This cam
paign also developed the earnest support of several
Psi U's in the area who were to play a part in selling
the idea to the eastern Chapters where the general
trend was against expansion.
By 1906 the Aztec Club had prepared its first peti
tion to the Psi Upsilon fraternity at its Convention
held at the Beta Beta Chapter at Trinity College,
Hartford, Conn. The petition was quite formal in for
mat. It included a history of the university, a run
down on all of the membership of the club and the
endorsement by letter of many members of Psi Upsi
lon. The petition was denied, but it did cause an in
tense interest on the part of many individual mem
bers of Psi Upsilon as well as the Chapters in and
around the area, from the Phi to the Mu. All seemed
to come away from their visits satisfied that the Aztec
Club should become a Chapter of Psi Upsilon.
The Aztec Club presented a second petition in 1907.
It received even greater support among the existing
Chapters but not in sufficient number to be approved.
By this time the enthusiasm of the undergraduate
members was increasing. There was, however, a grow
ing doubt among the Psi U Alumni in the area as to
whether the expansion should be supported. This
doubt resulted in the formation of an investigatory
group in Chicago which did a serious study of the
subject and came to the conclusion that the doubts
were without foundation. They made it knovra that
this was the decision of the group and that it was
unanimous.
History reveals that a small group from the Psi
Upsilon Club of Chicago, who had been members of
the investigating committee, and selected because of
their original open opposition to the petition of the
Aztec Club, turned up in the East visiting the several
Chapters and proclaiming their confirmed interest in
the success of the petition of the Aztec Club. At the
1908 Convention held at the Delta, the petition re
ceived the support of all but two Chapters.
By the time the 1909 Convention was convened in
June, at the Omega Chapter, the two hold out Chap
ters had relented and as a result the Convention
recommended the acceptance of the Aztec Club as a
Chapter of Psi Upsilon. That action was preliminary
to a long process whereby the action of the Conven
tion had to be ratified by all of the Chapters before
it could become official and final. It was not rmtil
April 26, 1910 that the Aztec Club received notice
that all of the Chapters had ratified the action of the
Convention and that there was now a Chapter of Psi
Upsilon to be installed at the University of Illinois.
It took those who were active members of the Aztec
Club exactly thirty-two days to get prepared for the
installation ceremony which included the presentation
of the active members at the Altar of Psi Upsilon in
accordance wdth the ceremony provided for in the
Constitution of Psi Upsilon. In addition to the active
Brothers, practically all of the members of the Aztec
Club who had participated in the eight year effort to
receive acceptance at the hands of Psi Upsilon were
also present.
Since that momentous occasion of May 28, 1910,
the Omicron has occupied three Chapter Houses in
cluding the present beautiful home on the campus.
This house is owned by the Alumni Association of the
Omicron, which was incorporated in 1918. It is to this
same association, with its well planned financial pro
gram, that made it possible for the Chapter to move
into its present home. The association has remained
strong and active and is one of the many reasons
why the Omicron Chapter is one of the outstanding
Chapters of the Fraternity.
The type of young men who foregathered in 1903
to develop into the Aztec Club most certainly were
of the finest types that could be found on the college
campus. Their example has been followed down
through the years and, as a result, it has been said
from sources outside the Chapter that it is the lead
ing fraternity on the campus of the University of Illi
nois and has been for many, many years.
In an effort to present a brief history of the Omi
cron Chapter it becomes necessary to state that there
have been many prominent Brothers associated with
the development, growth and successes of this well
founded Chapter. One cannot close any such epito

and John H. Parker, Omicron '28. Brother Morton
served for many years on the Executive Council and
was one of the most fascinating of public speakers

Bob Kaiser obtained his A.B. in economics at Dart

also a very active brother in the Zeta Chapter, pledg

and saw combat with General Patton's Third Army
in Europe. He remained in the Active Reserve until
1962 when he retired as Lieutenant Colonel after 22
years of active and reserve service.
